notes:
1. Nature of Indian Anti-Colonial Agitation

  • The Indian freedom struggle used several methods rather than a single uniform strategy.
  • Methods changed according to:
  • Political conditions.
  • Leadership.
  • Colonial repression.
  • Social participation.
  • Immediate political objectives.
  • Peaceful constitutional activity, economic resistance, mass mobilisation and other forms often existed simultaneously.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian National Movement → Multiple Methods + Changing Strategies

2. Main Categories of Agitation

Important modes included:

  • Constitutional agitation.
  • Petitions and representations.
  • Political associations.
  • Legislative intervention.
  • Press and journalism.
  • Public meetings and processions.
  • Swadeshi.
  • Boycott.
  • National education.
  • Hartal.
  • Picketing.
  • Labour strikes.
  • Peasant economic resistance.
  • Non-Cooperation.
  • Civil Disobedience.
  • Constructive work.
  • Symbolic protest.
  • International propaganda.
  • Electoral participation.

3. Constitutional Agitation

  • Constitutional agitation was the principal method of the early organised nationalist leadership.
  • Leaders attempted to obtain reforms through legal and institutional channels.
📌 Must-Memorise

Early Moderate Politics → Constitutional Agitation

4. Constitutional Methods

They included:

  • Petitions.
  • Memorials.
  • Resolutions.
  • Deputations.
  • Legislative speeches.
  • Parliamentary lobbying.

5. Petitions

  • A petition formally communicated grievances or demands to the government.
  • Early nationalists frequently submitted petitions to:
  • Viceroys.
  • Provincial governments.
  • British Parliament.

6. Memorials

  • Memorials were detailed written representations explaining political or administrative grievances.

7. Deputations

  • Nationalist leaders sometimes travelled to Britain to explain Indian demands directly to British politicians and public opinion.

8. Resolutions

  • Political associations and Congress sessions passed formal resolutions demanding administrative and constitutional reforms.

9. "Prayer, Petition and Protest"

  • Early Moderate politics is commonly summarised through the expression:
  • Prayer.
  • Petition.
  • Protest.
📌 Must-Memorise

Moderates → Prayer + Petition + Protest

10. Moderate Objective

  • Moderates initially sought gradual political reform rather than immediate revolutionary overthrow of British rule.

11. Political Education

  • Even where immediate reforms were limited, constitutional agitation helped create:
  • Political awareness.
  • All-India discussion.
  • A common vocabulary of rights.

12. Dadabhai Naoroji

  • Dadabhai Naoroji combined constitutional agitation with economic criticism of colonial rule.
🔗 Key Link

Naoroji → Economic Argument + Constitutional Advocacy

13. Gopal Krishna Gokhale

  • Gokhale used legislative councils and detailed speeches to question colonial financial and administrative policies.

14. Legislative Agitation

  • Legislative councils became another arena of nationalist opposition.

15. Questions and Debates

Nationalist representatives used councils to:

  • Question expenditure.
  • Criticise taxation.
  • Demand education reform.
  • Expose administrative failures.

16. Limit of Legislative Power

  • Colonial legislatures did not possess full democratic authority.
  • Nationalists nevertheless used them as political platforms.

17. Political Associations

  • Political associations enabled people with similar demands to organise collectively.

18. Pre-Congress Associations

Important examples included:

  • Indian Association.
  • Poona Sarvajanik Sabha.
  • Madras Mahajana Sabha.
  • Bombay Presidency Association.

19. Madras Mahajana Sabha

  • Madras Mahajana Sabha became an important centre of organised political activity in the Madras Presidency.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Madras Mahajana Sabha → Early Political Association

20. Importance of Associations

They helped create:

  • Leadership networks.
  • Public meetings.
  • Political resolutions.
  • Regional coordination.

21. Indian National Congress

  • The establishment of the INC provided an all-India platform for several modes of constitutional and mass agitation.

22. Public Meetings

  • Public meetings were among the simplest and most effective methods of political mobilisation.

23. Functions of Public Meetings

They were used to:

  • Explain political issues.
  • Pass resolutions.
  • Raise funds.
  • Mobilise volunteers.
  • Spread boycott campaigns.

24. Political Oratory

  • Public speaking became particularly important before mass electronic communication existed.

25. Subramania Siva

  • Subramania Siva became famous in Tamil Nadu for nationalist public speeches.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Subramania Siva → Political Oratory

26. Processions

  • Political processions made nationalist demands visible in public spaces.

27. Demonstrations

  • Demonstrations were organised against:
  • Colonial laws.
  • Government commissions.
  • Arrests.
  • Repressive policies.

28. Black-Flag Protest

  • Black flags were sometimes used to signify rejection or opposition to colonial officials and commissions.

29. Slogans

  • Short political slogans helped convert complex demands into memorable mass messages.

30. Political Songs

  • Songs were particularly useful in mobilising people who were not regular newspaper readers.

31. Nationalist Poetry

  • Poetry served as political agitation by creating emotional identification with:
  • Freedom.
  • Motherland.
  • Sacrifice.

32. Bharathiar

  • Subramania Bharathiar used poetry and journalism as major weapons of nationalism.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Bharathiar → Poetry + Journalism as Agitation

33. Political Journalism

  • Newspapers became one of the most influential modes of nationalist agitation.

34. Functions of the Press

Nationalist newspapers:

  • Exposed colonial policies.
  • Reported protests.
  • Spread nationalist ideas.
  • Linked distant regions.
  • Criticised repression.

35. Vernacular Press

  • Indian-language newspapers made political ideas accessible beyond English-educated elites.

36. Colonial Press Control

  • British authorities frequently used:
  • Security deposits.
  • Censorship.
  • Prosecution.
  • Confiscation

against nationalist publications.

37. Vernacular Press Act

  • The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 became an important example of colonial restrictions on the Indian-language press.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vernacular Press Act → 1878

38. Important Newspaper Method

Examples include:

  • Kesari → Tilak.
  • Al-Hilal → Maulana Azad.
  • India → Bharathiar.
  • Young India → Gandhi.
⚠️ TNPSC Caution

Detailed biographies of these leaders belong to their dedicated chapters.

39. Swadeshi as a Mode

  • Swadeshi meant deliberate preference for goods and enterprises produced or controlled by Indians.
📌 Must-Memorise

Swadeshi → Promote Indigenous Goods and Enterprise

40. Economic Nationalism

  • Swadeshi converted everyday economic decisions into political action.

41. Purpose of Swadeshi

It aimed to:

  • Reduce dependence on foreign goods.
  • Strengthen indigenous industries.
  • Promote economic self-reliance.

42. Indigenous Enterprise

  • Swadeshi could involve creation of:
  • Indian industries.
  • Banks.
  • Insurance companies.
  • Transport enterprises.

43. V.O. Chidambaranar

  • V.O.C.'s Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company was a major Tamil example of economic Swadeshi.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

V.O.C. → Economic Swadeshi

44. Boycott

  • Boycott meant deliberately refusing to purchase, use or participate in something connected with colonial rule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Boycott → Deliberate Withdrawal

45. Economic Boycott

  • Foreign goods, especially imported cloth, were common targets.

46. Institutional Boycott

Boycott could also extend to:

  • Government schools.
  • Courts.
  • Legislative councils.
  • Colonial ceremonies.

47. Swadeshi vs Boycott

Swadeshi:

  • Positive promotion of Indian alternatives.

Boycott:

  • Refusal of foreign or colonial alternatives.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Swadeshi → Use Indian Boycott → Reject Foreign

48. Foreign Cloth

  • Foreign cloth became one of the most visible symbols of colonial economic dependence.

49. Picketing Foreign-Cloth Shops

  • Volunteers could stand outside shops and peacefully persuade people not to purchase foreign cloth.

50. Bonfires of Foreign Cloth

  • Public burning of foreign cloth became a symbolic expression of economic resistance.

51. National Education

  • National education emerged as another form of anti-colonial agitation.
📌 Must-Memorise

National Education → Alternative to Colonial Education

52. Objective of National Education

It sought to provide:

  • Indian-controlled institutions.
  • National history.
  • National values.
  • Greater intellectual independence.

53. Student Boycott

  • Students sometimes withdrew from government institutions and joined national schools.

54. National Colleges

  • National colleges became centres for both:
  • Education.
  • Political awakening.

55. Hartal

  • A hartal was a voluntary suspension of normal commercial and public activity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hartal → General Voluntary Closure

56. Forms of Hartal

A hartal could involve:

  • Shops closing.
  • Work stopping.
  • Public gatherings.
  • Processions.

57. Political Purpose

  • Hartals demonstrated collective public opposition without necessarily attacking government property.

58. Strike

  • A strike occurred when workers collectively stopped work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Strike → Workers Stop Work

59. Economic Strike

  • Workers could strike over:
  • Wages.
  • Hours.
  • Working conditions.

60. Political Strike

  • A strike could also express solidarity with nationalist demands or political prisoners.

61. Coral Mill Example

  • V.O.C.'s support for the Tuticorin Coral Mill workers demonstrated how labour agitation could intersect with nationalism.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

V.O.C. → Labour + Nationalism

62. Hartal vs Strike

Hartal:

  • Wider closure involving shops and public activity.

Strike:

  • Primarily workers stopping labour.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Hartal ≠ Strike

63. Picketing

  • Picketing involved peaceful presence outside a targeted place to persuade people not to enter or purchase particular goods.

64. Main Targets

Common targets included:

  • Foreign-cloth shops.
  • Liquor shops.

65. Women's Participation

  • Picketing gave women an important visible role in nationalist mass politics.

66. Liquor-Shop Picketing

  • Prohibition campaigns sometimes became linked with nationalist constructive activity.

67. Periyar's Congress Phase

  • During his Congress period, Periyar participated in prohibition-related agitation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Periyar's Early Congress Phase → Prohibition Agitation

68. No-Tax Resistance

  • Refusal to pay certain taxes could become a method of organised political pressure.

69. Principle

  • Tax refusal challenged the government's ability to claim unquestioned obedience.

70. No-Revenue Campaign

  • Agricultural communities could refuse land revenue where payment was considered unjust or impossible.

71. No-Rent Campaign

  • Tenants could refuse rent as part of organised agrarian protest.

72. Economic Risk

Participants could face:

  • Confiscation.
  • Eviction.
  • Arrest.
  • Property attachment.

73. Peasant Agitation

  • Peasants organised against:
  • High revenue.
  • Rent.
  • Plantation exploitation.
  • Debt.
  • Landlord oppression.

74. Importance

  • Peasant agitation greatly expanded the social base of nationalism.

75. Labour Agitation

  • Workers brought industrial grievances into the anti-colonial political sphere.

76. Workers' Methods

They used:

  • Strikes.
  • Demonstrations.
  • Unions.
  • Public meetings.

77. Trade Unions

  • Organised trade unions made industrial action more systematic.

78. Student Agitation

Students participated through:

  • Boycott of classes.
  • Processions.
  • National schools.
  • Volunteer work.
  • Distribution of political literature.

79. Youth Organisations

  • Youth associations helped recruit and politically educate younger nationalists.

80. Women's Agitation

Women participated through:

  • Picketing.
  • Processions.
  • Public speeches.
  • Fundraising.
  • Boycott.
  • Law-breaking campaigns.

81. Expansion of Nationalism

  • Increasing participation by women, students, workers and peasants transformed nationalism from an elite political campaign into a much broader movement.

82. Non-Cooperation as a Method

  • Non-Cooperation meant deliberately withdrawing voluntary assistance from an unjust government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Cooperation → Refuse to Cooperate

83. Forms of Non-Cooperation

It could include withdrawal from:

  • Government institutions.
  • Titles.
  • Schools.
  • Courts.
  • Councils.

84. Important Boundary

  • The historical development of Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement, its causes, programme and withdrawal will be treated under Chapter 28 — Growth of Satyagraha.

85. Civil Disobedience as a Method

  • Civil Disobedience meant openly and deliberately violating an unjust law while accepting legal consequences.
📌 Must-Memorise

Civil Disobedience → Deliberately Break an Unjust Law

86. Non-Cooperation vs Civil Disobedience

Non-Cooperation:

  • Refuse assistance.

Civil Disobedience:

  • Violate a specific law.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Withdraw Cooperation vs Break Unjust Law

87. Important Boundary

  • Salt Satyagraha, Dandi, Vedaranyam and the wider Civil Disobedience Movement are not developed here.
  • Their place in the evolution of Satyagraha belongs to Chapter 28.

88. Satyagraha — Identification Only

  • Satyagraha was Gandhi's distinctive philosophy and method based on:
  • Truth.
  • Non-violence.
  • Self-suffering.
📌 Must-Memorise

Satyagraha → Truth + Non-Violence + Self-Suffering

89. Chapter Boundary for Satyagraha

  • This chapter identifies Satyagraha only as one mode of agitation.
  • Its origin, development, stages and major movements are reserved fully for Chapter 28.

90. Fasting

  • Fasting was sometimes used as a form of moral or political pressure.

91. Gandhian Fast

  • Gandhi interpreted fasting as an act of self-suffering and moral discipline.

92. Hunger Strike

  • Political prisoners also used hunger strikes to demand:
  • Better treatment.
  • Political-prisoner status.
  • Prison reforms.

93. Fast vs Hunger Strike

  • The terms can overlap physically but arose from different political contexts and moral frameworks.

94. Constructive Programme

  • Some nationalist leaders argued that resistance should be accompanied by positive social reconstruction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Constructive Programme → Build Alternatives, Not Only Protest

95. Major Constructive Activities

They included:

  • Khadi.
  • Village industries.
  • National education.
  • Sanitation.
  • Social reform.

96. Khadi

  • Khadi became both:
  • An economic practice.
  • A political symbol.

97. Charkha

  • The spinning wheel symbolised indigenous production and economic self-reliance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Charkha → Swadeshi + Self-Reliance

98. Constructive Resistance

  • Building Indian alternatives reduced dependence on colonial institutions.

99. Symbolic Protest

  • Political movements frequently relied on symbols capable of communicating complex ideas quickly.

100. Important Symbols

Examples included:

  • National flag.
  • Khadi.
  • Charkha.
  • Political songs.
  • National days.

101. Flag Hoisting

  • Hoisting a nationalist flag could become a direct assertion of political identity.

102. Tiruppur Kumaran

  • Tiruppur Kumaran became an important Tamil symbol of sacrifice associated with the national flag.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tiruppur Kumaran → Kodi Kaththa Kumaran

103. National Days

  • Observing specific days collectively helped build:
  • National unity.
  • Political memory.
  • Public mobilisation.

104. Returning Honours

  • Renouncing colonial honours was another form of symbolic protest.

105. Purpose

  • It publicly rejected the moral legitimacy of colonial recognition.

106. Courtroom Protest

  • Nationalists sometimes used colonial trials as platforms to explain their political principles.

107. Political Defence

  • Statements made in courts could circulate through the press and reach a larger audience.

108. Prison as an Arena of Protest

  • Imprisonment did not necessarily end political agitation.
  • Prisoners protested:
  • Conditions.
  • Racial discrimination.
  • Restrictions on reading.
  • Treatment of political prisoners.

109. Social Boycott

  • In some movements, social pressure was used against people who openly violated collective boycott decisions.

110. Caution on Coercion

  • Nationalist leaders differed over how much social pressure was ethically acceptable.
  • Gandhian politics insisted that participation should remain fundamentally non-violent.

111. Electoral Participation

  • Elections and legislative participation could themselves become political strategies.

112. Council Boycott vs Council Entry

  • Different nationalist groups sometimes disagreed over whether to:
  • Boycott colonial legislatures.
  • Enter them and challenge the government from within.

113. Swarajist Strategy

  • Swarajists favoured entry into legislatures to expose and obstruct colonial administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Swarajists → Council Entry + Obstruction

114. C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru

  • C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru became the most important leaders of this strategy.

115. No-Changers

  • Other Congress leaders preferred continued constructive work and boycott rather than council entry.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Swarajists vs No-Changers → Difference in Method, Not Ultimate Anti-Colonial Goal

116. Provincial Ministries

  • Later, nationalist participation in provincial elections allowed Congress to demonstrate its capacity to govern.

117. Resignation as Protest

  • Resigning from elected office could itself become a form of political agitation.

118. International Propaganda

  • Indian nationalists carried their struggle beyond India.
📌 Must-Memorise

International Agitation → Influence Foreign Public Opinion

119. Methods Abroad

They used:

  • Public speeches.
  • Associations.
  • Newspapers.
  • Meetings with foreign politicians.
  • International conferences.

120. Britain

  • Britain became an important centre because colonial policy was ultimately decided there.

121. United States and Europe

  • Indian leaders also sought support in:
  • United States.
  • France.
  • Germany.
  • Other European countries.

122. Purpose of International Agitation

It aimed to show that:

  • Indian nationalism was not a local disturbance.
  • Colonial rule was an international political and moral issue.

123. Militant/Armed Resistance — Identification Only

  • A section of the national movement adopted:
  • Secret organisation.
  • Revolutionary violence.
  • Armed resistance.
⚠️ Important Boundary

The organisations, personalities, cases and chronology belong entirely to:

Chapter 29 — Militant Movements.

124. What Chapter 27 Will Not Cover from Militant History

Not developed here:

  • Anushilan Samiti.
  • Jugantar.
  • Abhinav Bharat.
  • Ghadar.
  • Kakori.
  • HRA.
  • HSRA.
  • Saunders assassination.
  • Assembly Bomb Case.
  • Vanchinathan.
  • Revolutionary bomb cases.
  • INA's armed strategy.

These belong to Chapter 29.

125. Communal Mobilisation — Excluded

  • Communal political mobilisation is not treated here as a general mode of nationalist agitation because it belongs to a separate political development.
⚠️ Important Boundary

All detailed material on:

  • Muslim League.
  • Separate electorates.
  • Hindu-Muslim political division.
  • Two-Nation Theory.
  • Pakistan Resolution.
  • Direct Action.
  • Partition.

belongs exclusively to Chapter 30 — Communalism and Partition.

126. Tamil Nadu — Agitation Methods

Tamil Nadu provides clear examples of several different modes:

  • V.O.C. → Economic Swadeshi.
  • Bharathiar → Journalism and poetry.
  • Subramania Siva → Public oratory.
  • Rajaji → Gandhian law-breaking method.
  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi → Women's mass participation.
  • Tiruppur Kumaran → Symbolic flag protest.
  • Kamarajar → Congress organisation and mass mobilisation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tamil Nadu → Multiple Anti-Colonial Methods

127. V.O.C. — Method

  • V.O.C.'s distinctive method was to directly challenge British economic control through indigenous enterprise.

128. Bharathiar — Method

  • Bharathiar mobilised nationalist feeling through:
  • Poetry.
  • Journalism.
  • Political writing.

129. Subramania Siva — Method

  • Subramania Siva used mass speeches and touring to spread nationalist ideas.

130. Tiruppur Kumaran — Method

  • Tiruppur Kumaran represents the power of:
  • Processions.
  • National flags.
  • Political martyrdom.

131. Rajaji — Method

  • Rajaji represents disciplined Gandhian Civil Disobedience in Tamil Nadu.
⚠️ Boundary

The Vedaranyam campaign itself will be used only where necessary under the growth of Satyagraha in Chapter 28, rather than repeated here in detail.

132. Evolution of Political Participation

The broad trend of the national movement was from:

Educated political advocacy → Economic resistance → Public mobilisation → Mass participation

🔗 TNPSC Key Concept

Freedom Struggle → Progressive Expansion of Political Participation

133. Different Methods Could Coexist

  • Constitutional leaders and mass agitators were not always active in completely separate periods.
  • Legislative politics, journalism, boycott and mass agitation often operated together.

134. Change of Method

  • A leader or organisation could change its preferred method as political circumstances changed.

135. Strategy vs Objective

  • Leaders could disagree strongly over methods while sharing the objective of greater Indian self-government or independence.

136. Moderate vs Assertive Method

Moderates generally emphasised:

  • Constitutional pressure.

Assertive nationalists added greater emphasis on:

  • Boycott.
  • Swadeshi.
  • Mass mobilisation.

137. Gandhian Expansion

  • Gandhi later developed non-violent mass resistance into a much broader and more disciplined system.
⚠️ Boundary

Detailed Gandhi/Satyagraha development → Chapter 28.

138. Revolutionary Alternative

  • Other nationalists concluded that colonial rule could not be defeated through constitutional or non-violent methods alone.
⚠️ Boundary

Detailed revolutionary response → Chapter 29.

139. Social Base

Different methods attracted different sections:

  • Constitutional politics → Educated middle classes.
  • Swadeshi → Consumers, merchants, producers.
  • Strikes → Workers.
  • Agrarian resistance → Peasants.
  • Student boycott → Youth.
  • Picketing → Strong women's participation.
  • Mass political movements → Multiple social groups.

140. Importance of Leadership

  • Organisation and political discipline determined whether a protest remained limited or became a mass movement.

141. Colonial Response

British responses included:

  • Arrest.
  • Censorship.
  • Prosecution.
  • Fines.
  • Confiscation.
  • Police force.

142. Repression and Mobilisation

  • Repression sometimes discouraged participation.
  • At other times it produced:
  • Sympathy.
  • Wider mobilisation.
  • Martyrdom symbols.

143. Communication

Successful agitation depended on communication through:

  • Newspapers.
  • Posters.
  • Leaflets.
  • Songs.
  • Speeches.
  • Volunteers.

144. Volunteers

  • Volunteer organisations helped maintain:
  • Discipline.
  • Communication.
  • Crowd organisation.
  • Boycott campaigns.

145. Fundraising

  • Political agitation required funds for:
  • Publications.
  • Meetings.
  • National institutions.
  • Volunteer networks.

146. Nationalist Consumer

  • Swadeshi transformed the consumer into a political participant.

147. Nationalist Student

  • National education and boycotts transformed students into political participants.

148. Nationalist Worker

  • Strikes brought workers into political mobilisation.

149. Nationalist Woman

  • Picketing and public demonstrations opened major new spaces for women's political participation.

150. Nationalist Peasant

  • Revenue and agrarian protests linked rural economic grievances with larger political demands.

151. Why Different Modes Matter

  • The strength of Indian nationalism came partly from its ability to turn ordinary activities into political acts:
  • Buying.
  • Working.
  • Studying.
  • Paying taxes.
  • Wearing clothes.
  • Attending meetings.

152. Everyday Politics

  • Nationalism gradually moved from annual political meetings into everyday social and economic life.

153. Core Concept

A mode of agitation can therefore be understood as:

The practical method through which political opposition is expressed and pressure is created.

154. Essential Comparisons

Constitutional agitation → Seek reform through institutions.

Swadeshi → Promote indigenous alternatives.

Boycott → Withdraw from foreign goods or institutions.

Hartal → Broad voluntary closure.

Strike → Workers stop work.

Picketing → Peaceful persuasion at targeted locations.

Non-Cooperation → Withdraw assistance from unjust government.

Civil Disobedience → Openly violate an unjust law.

Constructive work → Build social and economic alternatives.

International propaganda → Seek foreign public support.

155. TNPSC Traps

  • Moderates → Constitutional methods.
  • Prayer, Petition and Protest → Moderate method.
  • Swadeshi → Promotion of indigenous goods.
  • Boycott → Refusal of foreign goods/institutions.
  • Swadeshi and boycott are related but not identical.
  • National education → Alternative Indian-controlled education.
  • Hartal and strike are not identical.
  • Hartal → Wider voluntary closure.
  • Strike → Workers stop work.
  • Picketing → Persuasion outside targeted places.
  • Non-Cooperation → Withdraw cooperation.
  • Civil Disobedience → Break an unjust law.
  • Satyagraha is broader than simply refusing cooperation.
  • Detailed Satyagraha history belongs to Chapter 28.
  • Revolutionary/militant organisations belong to Chapter 29.
  • Communalism and Partition belong to Chapter 30.
  • Swarajists favoured council entry.
  • No-Changers generally continued boycott and constructive work.
  • Press and poetry were genuine modes of agitation.
  • V.O.C. → Economic Swadeshi.
  • Bharathiar → Journalism and poetry.
  • Subramania Siva → Public oratory.
  • Tiruppur Kumaran → Flag symbolism.

156. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Moderates → Constitutional.
  • Petition → Written demand.
  • Deputation → Direct representation.
  • Press → Political awareness.
  • Meeting → Public mobilisation.
  • Procession → Visible protest.
  • Swadeshi → Indian goods.
  • Boycott → Reject foreign.
  • National education → Indian institutions.
  • Hartal → General closure.
  • Strike → Workers stop.
  • Picketing → Persuasion.
  • No-tax → Economic resistance.
  • Non-Cooperation → Withdraw.
  • Civil Disobedience → Break law.
  • Satyagraha → Chapter 28.
  • Militancy → Chapter 29.
  • Communalism → Chapter 30.
  • Constructive work → Build alternatives.
  • Swarajists → Council entry.
  • International propaganda → Foreign opinion.
  • V.O.C. → Economic Swadeshi.
  • Bharathi → Journalism.
  • Siva → Speeches.
  • Kumaran → Flag.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is meant by a mode of agitation? → A practical method through which political opposition is expressed and pressure is created.

Did the Indian national movement use only one method? → No.

Which method dominated the early Moderate phase? → Constitutional agitation.

What were the main Moderate methods? → Petitions, resolutions, deputations and legislative criticism.

Which phrase commonly summarises Moderate methods? → Prayer, Petition and Protest.

What was the purpose of petitions? → To formally communicate grievances and demands to colonial authorities.

What was a deputation? → A group sent to directly present political demands to officials or politicians.

Why were legislative councils useful to nationalists? → They provided platforms to question colonial policies and expenditure.

Name an important early political association in Madras. → Madras Mahajana Sabha.

Why were public meetings important? → They spread political information and mobilised ordinary people.

Which Tamil nationalist was famous for public oratory? → Subramania Siva.

How did Bharathiar agitate against colonial rule? → Through poetry and journalism.

Why was the press important? → It exposed government policies and created political awareness.

Which colonial law of 1878 restricted the vernacular press? → Vernacular Press Act.

What does Swadeshi mean? → Promotion and use of indigenous goods and enterprises.

What does boycott mean? → Deliberate refusal to use foreign goods or participate in selected colonial institutions.

What is the difference between Swadeshi and boycott? → Swadeshi promotes Indian alternatives; boycott rejects foreign alternatives.

Which Tamil leader made shipping a form of Swadeshi resistance? → V.O. Chidambaranar.

What was national education? → Development of Indian-controlled educational institutions outside colonial influence.

What is a hartal? → Voluntary general closure of shops, business or normal activity.

What is a strike? → Collective stoppage of work by workers.

What is the difference between hartal and strike? → Hartal is a wider public closure; strike primarily involves workers stopping labour.

What is picketing? → Peacefully persuading people outside a shop or institution not to enter or purchase targeted goods.

Which shops were commonly picketed? → Foreign-cloth and liquor shops.

Why were women important in picketing? → It became one of the major forms through which women entered mass political activism.

What is no-tax agitation? → Organised refusal to pay specified government taxes.

What is no-rent agitation? → Organised refusal by tenants to pay rent.

How did peasants participate in agitation? → Through revenue resistance, rent struggles, meetings and collective mobilisation.

How did workers participate? → Through strikes, unions and political demonstrations.

How did students participate? → Through boycotts, processions and national educational institutions.

What does Non-Cooperation mean as a method? → Withdrawal of voluntary assistance from an unjust government.

What does Civil Disobedience mean? → Open and deliberate violation of an unjust law.

What is the easiest distinction? → Non-Cooperation withdraws cooperation; Civil Disobedience breaks an unjust law.

Will Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements be explained fully here? → No.

Where will their historical development be explained? → Chapter 28 — Growth of Satyagraha.

What is Satyagraha? → Gandhi's method based on truth, non-violence and self-suffering.

Is the full history of Satyagraha part of Chapter 27? → No.

Which chapter covers it? → Chapter 28.

What is fasting as agitation? → Voluntary self-denial used for moral or political pressure.

What is a political hunger strike? → Refusal of food, often by prisoners or activists, to press specific demands.

What was constructive work? → Building social and economic alternatives alongside political protest.

Name examples. → Khadi, village industries, education, sanitation and social reform.

What did khadi symbolise? → Swadeshi and self-reliance.

What did the charkha symbolise? → Indigenous production and Gandhian self-reliance.

How could national flags become political methods? → Flag hoisting publicly asserted nationalist identity.

Which Tamil martyr is associated with protecting the national flag? → Tiruppur Kumaran.

What is his popular title? → Kodi Kaththa Kumaran.

What is symbolic renunciation of honours? → Publicly returning or rejecting colonial titles as a form of protest.

How could colonial courts become political platforms? → Nationalists used trials and statements to explain their political ideas.

How could prisons become arenas of agitation? → Political prisoners protested conditions and demanded equal treatment.

What did Swarajists propose? → Enter colonial legislatures and obstruct government from within.

Who were major Swarajist leaders? → C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.

Who were the No-Changers? → Congress leaders who preferred constructive work and continued boycott rather than council entry.

Was participation in elections necessarily acceptance of colonial rule? → No.

How could resignation from office become agitation? → It publicly withdrew political cooperation and legitimacy.

What was international propaganda? → Campaigning abroad to influence foreign opinion in favour of Indian freedom.

Why was Britain an important centre? → Ultimate colonial political authority lay there.

Does Chapter 27 cover detailed revolutionary organisations? → No.

Which chapter does? → Chapter 29 — Militant Movements.

Should HRA, HSRA, Ghadar, Kakori and revolutionary bomb cases be dumped into Chapter 27? → No.

Where do they belong? → Chapter 29.

Does Chapter 27 cover Muslim League politics and Partition? → No.

Where do they belong? → Chapter 30 — Communalism and Partition.

What is V.O.C.'s main method to remember here? → Economic Swadeshi.

What is Bharathiar's main method? → Poetry and journalism.

What is Subramania Siva's main method? → Political speeches.

What is Tiruppur Kumaran's main symbolic association? → National flag protest.

What broad change occurred in nationalist agitation over time? → It expanded from educated constitutional politics into economic and mass participation involving students, workers, peasants and women.

What is the central TNPSC takeaway? → Different Modes of Agitation should be understood as the toolbox of the freedom struggle—constitutional pressure, press, meetings, Swadeshi, boycott, national education, hartals, strikes, picketing, economic resistance, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, constructive work, electoral tactics and international propaganda—without duplicating the detailed evolution of Satyagraha, militant organisations or the later history of communalism and Partition.
